catalog_quote: There is no contrastive stress in Coorg in the sense shown in English import (verb/noun). However, it is not entirely predictable from the word alone, as defined above. In order to state the occurrence of stress a phonological unit called the syllable has to be set up, compatible with the larger phonological unit, the word (i.e. every word is wholly made up of syllables). Then, every word-initial syllable has full stress; every word-final syllable has secondary stress. Word-medially, a syllable has full stress if it contains a long vowel nucleus, or a short vowel nucleus followed by a geminate consonant cluster (the first consonant of the cluster being separated from the second by the syllable boundary). new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and word-initial: the first syllable of every (phonological) word carries full/main stress (p. 374: 'one main stress, on the first syllable, which contains the root vowel'). Additionally any word-medial heavy syllable (long vowel, or short vowel + first half of a geminate) also receives full stress, light medial syllables are unstressed, and the word-final syllable carries secondary stress. Forms with two adjacent initial full stresses (e.g. /ku:+kudike/) are analysed as containing an internal word boundary, each part then obeying the initial-stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Every word-final syllable has secondary stress; word-medial heavy syllables (long V, or short V closed by a geminate) carry full stress alongside the initial syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds/complex forms such as /ku:kudike/ 'large cooking vessel' show full stress on the first two syllables; Garman posits an internal word boundary /+/ (/ku:+kudike/), noting /+/ usually coincides with a morpheme boundary; where the pattern is predictable from weight (e.g. /nu:putti/) no boundary is marked. Emphatic stress in a 'continuative' form is mentioned separately (p. ~50). Loans aside, no consonant-final words.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word, defined (sec. 1.3, p. 32) as potentially pause-bounded; uninflected noun (subjective singular) and verb (2sg imperative) forms are single words, and inflected forms showing one main stress count as one word. Data mainly from Karada village (c. 10 mi W of Virajpet, South Coorg) plus a Mercara speaker, fieldwork 1968.
new_statements.identity_note: Garman describes 'Coorg' = Kodava/Kodagu [kfa], koda1255; data chiefly from Karada village near Virajpet (South Kodagu, the area Coorgs regard as the heartland of the language) with initial work with a Mercara-raised speaker of the same family; no separate Glottolog dialect code applies. Balakrishnan's 'Kodagu' (Annamalai) is the same language (fieldwork around Mercara 1968-74).

new_statements.quote: The favoured syllable pattern of the word (free form) in Dravidian is (C)V̄CV/(C)VCCV/(C)VCVCV (three morae each). The other types are infrequent. There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants. [...] [p. 28:] Short vowels in non-root syllables (in unaccented position) tend to be lost.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial-syllable stress, initial stress) and as Garman 1973 ('every word-initial syllable has full stress', no contrastive stress). Krishnamurti's sentence is a generalization over the whole family, not a Kodagu-specific description; it adds the explicit claim that stress is non-phonemic in every Dravidian language and that non-initial long vowels are louder, but says nothing about Garman's final-syllable secondary stress. Honesty note on access: the listed archive.org open copy (micro_IA41153650_0573) is a one-page ERIC microfiche 'Document Resume' card (ED 475 049): abstract only, 'Document Not Available From EDRS', no book text (abstract or snippet o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement, not Kodagu-specific: stress is not phonemic anywhere in Dravidian; the initial syllable of the word carries stress (loudness) regardless of whether it is short or long; a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (a weight-conditioned secondary prominence, not a shift of main stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated as such; the only related remark is that a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels (p. 27). Nothing on final-syllable secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kodagu. The Google Books snippet of the ch. 2 discussion ('first syllable is stressed if it is long; otherwise, it is the penultimate syllable that carries stress, e.g. kuturu daughter.. palaka slate') concerns Telugu (Lisker & Krishnamurti 1991 data), not Kodagu.
new_statements.identity_note: Krishnamurti's stress statement is about the Dravidian family as a whole; his Kodagu entry (p. 23, '6. Kodagu (Coorgi, Kodagi, Kodava)', pop. 93,000, Kodagu district, sources Cole 1867, Emeneau fieldnotes 1935-8, Balakrishnan 1976/1977, Ebert 1996) contains no stress information. No particular Kodagu dialect is described.

sources.note: Sec. 1.4 'Stress' (pp. 32-33): no contrastive stress; every word-initial syllable has full stress, every word-final syllable secondary stress; word-medial syllables get full stress only if heavy (long vowel, or short vowel closed by the first half of a geminate); apparent exceptions handled by an internal word boundary /+/. Ch. 5 p. 374: a simple lexeme 'shows one main stress, on the first syllable, which contains the root vowel'; stress-assignment rule marks main stress on all root vowels. Verified against page images.
